analysis.one_liner: Requires stark, rotating health warnings and full ingredient disclosure on all tobacco products and their advertising.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it sat in two House subcommittees from April 1997 until the Congress ended in January 1999.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have replaced the aging cigarette warnings (unchanged since 1984) with blunt labels like "Cigarettes Kill" and "Cigarettes Are Addictive," printed large on both sides of the package, in Spanish as well as English, and covering a third of every tobacco ad. It would have forced makers to report all ingredients yearly, put a insert listing carcinogens inside every cigarette pack, publish ingredient information on a toll-free number and website, and let public-health nonprofits sue violators, with fines up to $100,000 per violation per day. It also stated that following the federal rules would not shield tobacco companies from lawsuits under state law.
analysis.who_benefits: Smokers and people tempted to start, especially teenagers, get far more honest information about what tobacco contains and does. Nonsmokers gain from warnings about secondhand smoke. Public-health nonprofits gain a legal tool to force compliance.

how_it_helps.text: Requires blunt new warnings — "Cigarettes Kill," "Cigarettes Are Addictive," "Smoking During Pregnancy Can Harm Your Baby" — in large type on the two most prominent sides of every package, one in Spanish [S3].

Requires every cigarette pack to contain an insert disclosing carcinogens and other dangerous ingredients, and manufacturers to report ingredients and nicotine, tar, and carbon monoxide yields annually, with public dissemination via a toll-free number and Internet site [S2] [S3].
Requires warnings covering 33% of the top of every tobacco advertisement, including billboards [S3].

Lets any nonprofit whose work includes reducing tobacco use sue to stop violations, with attorney's fees if it substantially prevails, and sets civil penalties up to $100,000 per violation per day [S3].
States that compliance with federal labeling law does not relieve anyone from liability under common law or state law, preserving smokers' and states' ability to sue [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Tobacco manufacturers bear the cost of new packaging, inserts, ingredient reporting, and fines for violations. Magazines, billboards, and other ad outlets give up a third of tobacco-ad space to warnings. Some compliance costs would flow into cigarette prices, which public-health advocates would count as a benefit since higher prices curb youth smoking.

drawbacks.text: The packaging, insert, and annual ingredient-reporting requirements impose real compliance costs on manufacturers, and the mandate that warnings fill 33% of every ad would cost magazines, billboards, and other outlets revenue from the roughly $5 billion-a-year tobacco ad market the bill itself cites [S3].

The bill relies on existing agencies and does not appropriate new enforcement funding, so its practical force would depend on the Secretary of Health and Human Services writing and enforcing regulations under tight deadlines [S3].

A good-faith objection: harsher labels on packages do not reach the many smokers' packs already on shelves, and evidence that warning-format changes alone substantially cut smoking is limited, so the bill's public-health payoff, while real, is uncertain relative to the economic disruption it would impose on tobacco-growing regions.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain is straightforward: consumers get dramatically more complete and more visible information about a product the bill calls the only one that kills when used as intended, at the cost of compliance expenses and ad revenue concentrated on tobacco companies and media outlets. The liability-preservation clause is the most consequential part beyond labeling, because it keeps state-law lawsuits alive. The bill is not badly designed, though its enforcement depends entirely on agency follow-through.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the House Commerce Committee, which passed it down to two subcommittees, and neither ever acted on it, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Martin Meehan introduced the bill on April 8, 1997, joined by six cosponsors split evenly between the parties, four Democrats and two Republicans [S1] [S4] [S5].
The House referred it to the Committee on Commerce on April 8, 1997, and on April 14 to two of its subcommittees, Telecommunications, Trade, and Consumer Protection, and Health and Environment [S5].
No further action was ever recorded; no hearing, no markup, no floor vote appears in the action history before the 105th Congress ended on January 3, 1999 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Tobacco manufacturers and the media outlets carrying their roughly $5 billion in annual advertising were spared the new warnings, disclosures, fines, and preserved lawsuit exposure.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Tobacco companies and their ad outlets

for.role: Cosponsor; senior member of the Commerce health subcommittee

for.name: Reps. Hansen, Riggs, Serrano, and Visclosky

against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: The committee never acted on the bill after referral; it sat in two subcommittees from April 14, 1997 until the Congress ended with no hearing, markup, or vote

against.name: Tobacco industry
against.role: Manufacturers and advertisers of cigarettes and spit tobacco
against.what_they_did: The bill's requirements would have hit this industry directly; the industry was widely engaged in opposing tobacco-control legislation during the 105th Congress

sides.party_line_note: The bill's small sponsorship was bipartisan — six cosponsors split four Democrats and two Republicans — but no votes ever occurred, so the partisan shape of the opposition was never recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have forced blunt rotating warnings on all packages and ads, an ingredient-and-carcinogen insert in every cigarette pack, annual ingredient reporting, fines up to $100,000 per violation per day, and explicitly preserved state-law liability. The industry's interest in killing it ran directly against the public's interest in knowing what is in the product.

industries.industry: Advertising and media outlets (magazines, billboards, point-of-purchase display)
industries.note: Every tobacco ad would have had to devote 33% of its space at the top to a warning label, cutting the space tobacco's roughly $5 billion annual ad budget could buy and the revenue outlets earn from it.
The bill gives any nonprofit working to reduce tobacco use standing to sue violators, with attorney's fees if it substantially prevails, creating a private enforcement tool.
